entities.name: Amenemhat Sénébef
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sekhemkare Amenemhat Senebef, an early pharaoh of Egypt's Thirteenth Dynasty, reigned briefly around 1777 BCE, marking a pivotal yet often overlooked transition in the late Middle Kingdom. His rule, preceding the full fragmentation into the Second Intermediate Period, is primarily attested through the Turin King List and limited epigraphic evidence, suggesting a period of continued royal authority, albeit one increasingly challenged by internal pressures. His existence confirms the dynastic continuity following the powerful Twelfth Dynasty, even as the central government's grip on the vast Egyptian state began to loosen.

During his short reign, Senebef likely inherited a state grappling with administrative decentralization and the growing autonomy of provincial nomarchs. While no grand building projects or military campaigns are definitively attributed to him, his appearance on the Turin King List as the second ruler of the Thirteenth Dynasty, after Sobekhotep I (or Wegaf, depending on interpretation), underscores his legitimate claim to the throne. His monumental presence is largely confined to a few stelae and scarabs, which, while scarce, provide invaluable chronological markers for Egyptologists attempting to reconstruct the complex succession of this turbulent era. The brevity of his rule, characteristic of many early Thirteenth Dynasty pharaohs, hints at an unstable political climate.
